name: What Counts as Protected Health Information
blurb: HIPAA definitions and de-identification for AI use.
title: What Counts as Protected Health Information
answer: Protected health information is individually identifiable information about a person's health, care or payment for care. HIPAA allows de-identified data to be used freely, either by removing 18 specified identifiers or by an expert determination that re-identification risk is very small.

reading.body:
HIPAA permits de-identified health data to be used freely, either by stripping 18 specified identifiers or by an expert determination that re-identification risk is very small.

The definition of protected health information turns on identifiability, not on sensitivity. Information about a person's health, care, or payment for care is protected only when it is individually identifiable. Remove that link and the data leaves the category entirely, which is why de-identification is the hinge on which most health AI training turns.

The two permitted routes are not equivalent in practice. Safe harbor is a fixed list of 18 identifiers, so it is mechanical and predictable. Expert determination is a judgment that re-identification risk is very small, which is the route the guidance points to for clinical notes, where free text defeats a checklist approach. For AI specifically, the distinction matters because training and testing corpora are usually built from exactly that kind of unstructured text.

What this does not cover is the rest of the compliance picture. It says nothing about how a model trained on de-identified data should be governed, what happens when outputs recombine into identifiable information, or how state law or the EU AI Act's high-risk deadlines interact with HIPAA. It also gives no numbers: no counts of covered entities, no breach statistics, no measure of how often either de-identification method is used.

The category boundary is identifiability, and identifiability is a property of the record, not of the model. A note stripped of the 18 identifiers is unprotected data even if it describes a rare disease, and a note with a full name attached is protected even if it says nothing clinically useful. That asymmetry is what makes de-identification attractive to anyone assembling a training corpus, and it is also what makes the choice of method consequential.

Safe harbor and expert determination fail in different directions. Safe harbor fails by leaving residual structure in the text, because a fixed list of 18 identifiers cannot anticipate every combination of date, place, and rare condition that narrows a record to one person. Expert determination fails by being a judgment, which means it can be defended or attacked but not verified against a list. The guidance points to expert determination for clinical notes for exactly this reason, and clinical notes are the substrate most AI training and testing corpora are built from.

The practical consequence is that the de-identification decision is made once, at corpus construction, and then inherited by everything downstream. A model trained on safe-harbor-stripped text carries whatever residual identifiability survived the checklist into every output it produces. Nothing in the definition of protected health information governs that output, and nothing in the definition tells you what to do when outputs recombine into something identifiable.

What is the difference between safe harbor and expert determination for de-identification?
Safe harbor removes 18 specified identifiers from the data. Expert determination is a judgment that re-identification risk is very small, and HHS guidance points to it for free text such as clinical notes.

Does de-identified data still count as protected health information?
No. Protected health information is individually identifiable information about a person's health, care, or payment for care, so removing the link to the individual takes the data out of the category.

Which de-identification method should be used for clinical notes used to train AI?
Expert determination, because clinical notes are hard to de-identify by safe harbor alone. The data does not specify any threshold, procedure, or reviewer qualification for making that determination.

What are the 18 identifiers that safe harbor removes?
The data does not list them. It states only that safe harbor is a fixed list of 18 specified identifiers.

Does HIPAA govern what a model does with de-identified data after training?
The data does not address this. It covers the definition of protected health information and the two de-identification methods, and says nothing about governance of models trained on de-identified data or about outputs that recombine into identifiable information.

How does the EU AI Act or state law interact with HIPAA here?
The data does not hold this. It references the Digital Omnibus and its 2026 amendments to the EU AI Act only as a related term, with no described interaction with HIPAA.
